title: Re'eh: rejoice together (Deuteronomy 16:11, 14)
hook: rejoice at the festival with the servant, the stranger, the orphan and the widow

segments.voice: Yesterday, shmita, the seventh-year release, and Hillel's fix. Your line was release. What did you let drop? Today is day five hundred, and fittingly, the Torah commands a party. Day five hundred.

A really good wedding. The music, the dancing, the food. Now look at who's there. Family, old friends, coworkers. Who isn't? The neighbor who lives alone. The new guy at work who doesn't know anyone yet. Nobody left them out on purpose. They just weren't on the list. A celebration tends to draw its circle around the people already loved. The Torah's festival law draws that circle, and then keeps going, naming people one by one until the guest list looks very different.
screen: `A REALLY GOOD WEDDING.` → `WHO WASN'T THERE?` → `THE CIRCLE KEEPS GOING.`

segments.voice: Deuteronomy sixteen walks through the three pilgrimage festivals: Passover, Shavuot, and Sukkot. For Shavuot and Sukkot, it commands joy. In the old Jewish translation, of Sukkot: "And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast." The Hebrew word for that joy is today's word, simcha. And then the guest list. Thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, and thy servants, and the Levite, who, Deuteronomy says elsewhere, has no portion of land, and the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your gates. Rashi, the medieval commentator, counts them in two groups of four. Four are yours: son, daughter, manservant, maidservant. Four are God's: the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, the widow. And he imagines God saying: if you make Mine happy, I'll make yours happy. Maimonides, in a line we met earlier in the year, makes it sharper. In his law code he writes that someone who locks the gates of his courtyard and eats and drinks with his family, but doesn't feed the poor and the grieving, isn't having the joy of a commandment at all. He's having the joy of his stomach. So in Jewish law, simcha isn't only a feeling you have. It's something you make, and you can't fully make it alone or only with your own. Joy, in this chapter, is measured partly by who else is at the table.
screen: `THREE FESTIVALS, AND A COMMAND TO REJOICE.` · `FOUR OF YOURS, FOUR OF MINE.` · `THE JOY OF HIS STOMACH.` · `WHO ELSE IS AT THE TABLE?` · then, large: `REJOICE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: include someone in a celebration. Settle, and breathe. You've reached five hundred days of this. That's worth a small celebration, and it's yours. Now think about the next gathering in your life: a birthday, a holiday meal, a Sabbath dinner, a game night, even coffee. Picture the table. Now picture Rashi's other four. Who in your life is the stranger, the one alone, the one grieving, the one without people nearby? Choose one to invite. The bell holds the time.
Simcha. Joy, the festival kind, commanded in Deuteronomy and made bigger by who you bring in.
Your line: rejoice together. Today, invite one person who wouldn't be on the usual list. Day five hundred.

screen: `DAY 500 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: RE'EH: AS YOU WERE BLESSED (DEUTERONOMY 16:17).`

howItsDone: Jewish law treats joy on the festivals, especially Sukkot, as a commandment, and some families make a point of inviting guests, newcomers and people who would otherwise be alone to holiday meals.

match.prompt: inside the guest list — tap the pairs.

myth: the Torah commands joy at the festivals
"And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast."
Maimonides says a family feast behind locked gates fulfills the joy of the festival
without feeding the poor and grieving, he calls it the joy of his stomach.
the Levite is on the guest list because he has no land of his own
along with the stranger, the orphan and the widow.

fork.setup: you're planning a festival meal. according to Deuteronomy, who's on the list?
options: your family, your workers, and the Levite, stranger, orphan and widow.
fork.reveal: Rashi counts four of yours and four of God's, and imagines God saying: make Mine happy, and I'll make yours happy.

original.note: Hebrew: joy, gladness. in Deuteronomy, the joy the festivals command.

trapdoor: what you thought: simcha means a happy occasion.
what it means: a joy you make, commanded, and measured partly by who else is at the table.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on 16:11 pairs four of yours with four of Mine; Maimonides, Laws of Festivals 6:18, calls a closed feast the joy of the stomach.

sources.quoted: And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast

Deuteronomy 16:14 opening quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; the guest list is paraphrased; verify.
Rashi on 16:11, 'four of yours corresponding to four of Mine'; paraphrased.
Maimonides, Hilchot Yom Tov 6:18, 'the joy of his stomach'; confirm halacha number.
16:11 refers to Shavuot and 16:14 to Sukkot; the command of joy for Passover is derived by the rabbis, not stated in this chapter.
